notes.text: The voice — Christ's voice, the word of grace revealed outwardly in the gospel, and inwardly by the Spirit of God. Leaping - He saith, leaping and skipping, to denote that Christ came readily, and swiftly, with great desire and pleasure and adds, upon the mountains and hills, to signify Christ's resolution to come in spite of all difficulties.

Like a roe — In swiftness. He is coming to me with all speed and will not tarry a moment beyond the proper season. He standeth behind - And while he doth for wise reasons forbear to come; he is not far from us. Both this and the following phrases may denote the obscure manner of Christ's manifesting himself to his people, under the law, in comparison of his discoveries in the gospel. The window - This phrase, and that through the lattess, intimate that the church does indeed see Christ, but, as through a glass, darkly, as it is said even of gospel-Revelations, 1 Cor. xiii, 12, which was much more true of legal administrations.

Spake — Invited me outwardly by his word, and inwardly by his Spirit. Rise up - Shake off sloth, and disentangle thyself more fully from all the snares of this world. Come - Unto me, and with me; follow me fully, serve me perfectly, labour for a nearer union, and more satisfying communion with me.

The winter — Spiritual troubles arising from a deep sense of the guilt of sin, the wrath of God, the curse of the law; all which made them afraid to come unto God. But, saith Christ, I have removed these impediments, God is reconciled; therefore cast off all discouragements, and excuses, and come to me.

The flowers — The communications of God's grace, the gifts, and graces, and comforts of the Holy Spirit, are vouchsafed unto, and appear in believers, as buds and blossoms do in the spring. The turtle - This seems particularly to be mentioned because it not only gives notice of the spring, but aptly represents the Spirit of God, which even the Chaldee paraphrast understands by this turtle, which appeared in the shape of a dove, and which worketh a dove-like meekness, and chastity, and faithfulness, in believers.
Her figs — Which it shoots forth in the spring.

glossa.text: *The voice of my beloved.* This is the voice which I heard adjuring the daughters of Jerusalem that they should not awaken me: I rejoice hearing his consoling voice, though I do not yet see his face; yet, my mind being lifted up to heaven, I taste beforehand some sweetness of the blessedness to come, even in this present life. *Leaping upon the mountains.* He leaps upon the mountains, and as it were sets his feet there, by which sign he is known to have been there, because it imitates him through his passion and through the manner of his life. He made a leap from heaven into the womb, from the womb into the manger, from the manger into the cross, from the cross into the sepulchre, from the sepulchre he returned into heaven. He it is who is lifted up above all mountains and hills, that is, above the heights of the saints, both the greater and the lesser. *Skipping over the hills.* On the *hills* the marks of his feet do not appear, but they received the shadow of him flying over: because although not as those greater ones, yet in some measure they imitate him and are visited by him, *Mountains* and *hills* are those who by a singular purity of mind pass beyond the common manner of life of the Church, as it were the flowering plain of the fields, and, withdrawing from the lowest things, contemplate the things above more nearly. In whom he *leaps,* because he illumines the hearts of the lofty with frequent visitation; and he abides not, but *leaps* and *skips over:* because this sweetness of contemplation is short and rare, because of the heaviness of the flesh, because the earthly habitation weighs down the mind that thinks upon many things.

*My beloved is like a roe.* Because he sees keenly, and dwells in the high places of the mountains, he leaps swiftly. Whence also he is more rarely seen by us: he ascends always from his nativity even to the bosom of the Father. *My beloved is like a roe.* And although by his divinity he so transcends all, yet he was made man, for me he was born of a Gentile and of the seed of the patriarchs. In the assumption of flesh and in his manhood he is compared to a *roe;* in the variety of virtues and of miracles to a *fawn.* The hart draws the serpent out of its caverns by the blowing of its nostrils, and, the destruction of the poison being overcome, delights in the food. Since in these little verses the loftiness of the contemplative life has been expressed, it remains to show the perfection of the active life, which is common to the whole Church. Whence follows. *Behold he standeth,* etc. *Behind the wall.* The wall which draws us away from the sight of him is the condition of mortality, which we deserved by sinning, we who were so created that, if we sinned not, all we the elect should behold the divine light unwearied: to the beholding of which very few of the more perfect now attain, with labour, purified by faith: but in this wall the mercy of God has made windows and lattices, whence he has made us to look forth, because to minds, although he weighed them down, he opened the grace of the knowledge of himself, and he looks upon us with the frequent light of his inspiration. Through the looking forth of which inspiration, because God does this chiefly, that he may call us from temporal things to the deserving of heavenly things, rightly is it subjoined: *Behold my beloved speaketh to me,* he who above admonished the daughters of Jerusalem to the guarding of my rest: he sends me to the tilling of the vineyards, showing me the opportunity. *Behind the wall.* Morally, if thou hast made thy building, God will come *behind the wall* of thine, *looking forth through the windows,* that is, through the five senses he carefully beholds; for where the Bridegroom looks not forth, death goes up: whence Jeremias: *Behold death is gone up through our windows ((Jer. IX))*; *through the nets.* All things are full of the nets of the devil, in which thou wouldst be taken, but that the Bridegroom subjected himself to the nets of the world, who eminently, and rending them asunder, might make a way, that thou mayest say: *Our soul hath been delivered as a sparrow out of the snare of the fowlers ((Psal. CXXIII))*. *Through the windows.* As the sun entering through the windows lights up the house, so Christ has enlightened us by the example and the admonition of the apostles. As through the *lattices,* that is, through small openings a small light enters, so an obscure knowledge through the prophets.

*Arise, make haste.* That is, break off contemplation, and labour for the winning of others; or, arise from the love of earthly things. Arise, all things have their time; he who but now was adjuring the daughters of Jerusalem not to disquiet his beloved: behold, he invites her to labour. *Arise, make haste.* ((GREG.)) When the soul is now led forth out of the body of corruption, for it the shower has passed, because the torpor of the present life has departed, and it is led forth to contemplate God in his substance, nor are the drops of words now needful, that the rain of preaching should be poured in. For what it was able to hear less, it shall see more fully. For then *the flowers appear in the earth,* when the soul has begun to taste beforehand certain first beginnings of sweetness out of the eternal life of blessedness, which things, going forth, she now smells in the flowers, and which, after she shall have gone forth, she shall have more abundantly in the fruit. *The time of cutting away is come.* Our cutting away then takes place when we forsake the unfruitful and hurtful corruption of the flesh, that we may be able to come to the fruit of the soul, which fruit is to us most abundant. For in the cutting away the barren branches are cut back, that those which are strong may bear fruit more abundantly. Therefore *arise,* because I, suffering for thee, have stilled the waves.

*Come.* To bestow also the care of salvation upon thy neighbours through the zeal of diligent preaching, that with a great company thou mayest deserve to be received unto the marriage. As if: thou believest that thou wilt come if thou art free for contemplation: but thou shalt come better through labour of this kind. It behoves thee to preach, because, since knowledge is now in thee, there is also in those to whom I send thee an opportunity of receiving.

*The rain is over.* I, rising from the dead, the tempest being checked, gave back tranquillity. Now it is easier to preach, since certain men are already converted, than before, when as yet no one had believed.

*The flowers. As if:* These, who now believe and now work good things, thou canst give as an example to others: these thou canst set before others for an example, who now suffer the pruning-hook that cuts back their vices. For thy own quiet thou oughtest not to let go preaching, because Christ, who was in great quiet with the Father, in a manner interrupted his quiet for preaching. *The time of pruning.* The useless branches of vain religion being now cut away, the hearts of men are prepared for the fruit of faith to come, now also the vices are cut away, because the time of the remission of sins is come. *The voice of the turtle is heard.* The Holy Spirit, when he speaks of the more hidden mysteries, and of things which many do not receive, is signified by the name of the turtle. Whence also he appears to Moses, and to him alone: when he treats of humble things which reach even to all, he is taken up under a dove, whence also at the Jordan, while many stood by, he appeared not in a turtle, but in a dove. *The voice of the turtle,* the voice of the apostles, or of any preachers whatsoever, who by their song announce the departure of winter and the coming of spring, who instead of a song render a lowly moan, who are lovers of chastity, who abide always upon the ridges of the mountains, or upon the tops of trees, and flee the company of men, while, set in the world in body, they have their conversation in the heavens, mindful of their sojourning and of the country promised to them.

*The fig tree.* He calls green figs the first and unripe figs, which are not fit for eating, which also, if they be shaken, fall at a light touch: therefore, when the turtle sounds, that is, when the apostles preach, the Synagogue put forth her green figs, that is, she cast away the unripe understanding of the legal observance. Or thus: the Synagogue brought forth the apostles, who should minister sweet food to those who believed them. And because, when the Synagogue put forth the apostles, the faith and the salvation of the whole world followed, rightly is it subjoined. *The vineyards in flower.* By the flowering, the beginnings of the manifold Churches, from that which was first planted at Jerusalem, from whose flower the juice pressed out makes a kind of drink suited to health and to delight, which gladdens the heart of man.

notes.text: Enditing — Hebrew. boileth, or bubbleth up like water over the fire. This denotes that the workings of his heart, were fervent and vehement, kindled by God's grace, and the inspiration of the Holy Ghost. Made - Have composed. Pen - He was only the pen or instrument in uttering this song; it was the spirit of God, by whose hand this pen was guided.

Fairer — Than all other men: which is most true of Christ; but not of Solomon; whom many have excelled, in holiness and righteousness, which is the chief part of the beauty celebrated in this psalm. Grace - God hath plentifully poured into thy mind and tongue the gift of speaking wisely, eloquently, and acceptably. Therefore - And because God hath so eminently qualified thee for rule, therefore he hath blessed thee with an everlasting kingdom.

glossa.text:
*It hath uttered forth.* ((AUG., HIER.)) For the Prophet speaks within, etc., *as far as* before that is which he is about to do. But the counsel of the Father is the Word.

*Good.* By which all good things were made. *I speak.* That is, I bring forth the Word: the same here as before; but he says that in that very word are all the works of God; whence: *What was made in him was life,* so that nothing may be in the work which was not first in the counsel. Of this it is said: *God hath spoken once.*

*A pen.* He compares the Word not to sound, which passes away, but to writing, which remains. Or, *swiftly,* because not one thing after another, but all things together in one eternal Word.

*Swiftly.* The power of prophecy, which does not under human torment devise what it divulges to others out of the secret of the Godhead.

*Beautiful in form.* ((CASS.)) He begins the praise of the bridegroom first from his form. *He hath blessed.* The former things the Prophet said in the person of God, these from his own; or all from himself. Or, *he uttereth forth the word,* who says a hymn to God.

*I speak my works.* ((AUG.)) to the praise of him who is from him. *Tongue, a pen.* Because what I say, I also write. Or, *swiftly:* because the things which I write are quickly to come.

((CASS.)) *In the lips.* Because, when he spoke, the world received the grace of reconciliation.

notes.text: No evil, but every good gift — Whatever tends to holiness. And every perfect gift - Whatever tends to glory. Descendeth from the Father of lights - The appellation of Father is here used with peculiar propriety. It follows, "he begat us." He is the Father of all light, material or spiritual, in the kingdom of grace and of glory. With whom is no variableness - No change in his understanding. Or shadow of turning - in his will. He infallibly discerns all good and evil; and invariably loves one, and hates the other. There is, in both the Greek words, a metaphor taken from the stars, particularly proper where the Father of lights is mentioned. Both are applicable to any celestial body, which has a daily vicissitude of day and night, and sometimes longer days, sometimes longer nights. In God is nothing of this kind. He is mere light. If there Is any such vicissitude, it is in ourselves, not in him.

Of his own will — Most loving, most free, most pure, just opposite to our evil desire, ver. 15. Begat he us - Who believe. By the word of truth - The true word, emphatically so termed; the gospel. That we might be a kind of first-fruits of his creatures - Christians are the chief and most excellent of his visible creatures; and sanctify the rest. Yet he says, A kind of - For Christ alone is absolutely the first-fruits.

Let every man be swift to hear — This is treated of from ver. 21 to the end of the next chapter. Slow to speak - Which is treated of in the third chapter. Slow to wrath - Neither murmuring at God, nor angry at his neighbour. This is treated of in the third, and throughout the fourth and fifth chapters.
The righteousness of God here includes all duties prescribed by him, and pleasing to him.

Therefore laying aside — As a dirty garment. All the filthiness and superfluity of wickedness - For however specious or necessary it may appear to worldly wisdom, all wickedness is both vile, hateful, contemptible, and really superfluous. Every reasonable end may be effectually answered without any kind or degree of it. Lay this, every known sin, aside, or all your hearing is vain. With meekness - Constant evenness and serenity of mind. Receive - Into your ears, your heart, your life. The word - Of the gospel. Ingrafted - In believers, by regeneration, ver. 18 and by habit, Heb. v, 14. Which is able to save your souls - The hope of salvation nourishes meekness.
Beholding his face in a glass — How exactly does the scripture glass show a man the face of his soul!
He beheld himself, and went away — To other business. And forgot - But such forgetting does not excuse.

But he that looketh diligently — Not with a transient glance, but bending down, fixing his eyes, and searching all to the bottom. Into the perfect law - Of love as established by faith. St. James here guards us against misunderstanding what St. Paul says concerning the "yoke and bondage of the law." He who keeps the law of love is free, John viii, 31, &c. He that does not, is not free, but a slave to sin, and a criminal before God, ver. 10. And continueth therein - Not like him who forgot it, and went away. This man - There is a peculiar force in the repetition of the word. Shall be happy - Not barely in hearing, but doing the will of God.

If any one be ever so religious — Exact in the outward offices of religion. And bridleth not his tongue - From backbiting, talebearing, evilspeaking, he only deceiveth his own heart, if he fancies he has any true religion at all.

The only true religion in the sight of God, is this, to visit — With counsel, comfort, and relief. The fatherless and widows - Those who need it most. In their affliction - In their most helpless and hopeless state. And to keep himself unspotted from the world - From the maxims, tempers, and customs of it. But this cannot be done, till we have given our hearts to God, and love our neighbour as ourselves.

glossa.text:
*Every gift,* etc. ((BED.)) After he had taught that vices are not to us from God, but from ourselves, etc., *as far as* the perfect gift can be understood.

*Nor of alteration.* No shadow shuts off his light, so as to send in any evils. Always the goods of light are in God, but his gifts in us are sometimes such as supervening sins overshadow.

*Of his own will.* Every good is from God, and you have not come to this by your own merits, but by the sole grace of the divine will. *That we might be some beginning,* etc. By this begetting let us not think that we are that which he himself is, but a certain primacy among creatures he granted to us by adoption. Whence another translator: *That we might be the firstfruits of his creatures.*

*Slow to anger.* Let no one be angry rashly and without cause, whether against sinning subjects, or against any brethren whatsoever, or against the prosperity of the wicked, because the ripeness of wisdom is not perceived save with a tranquil mind. And he who judges in anger, even if he judges justice, yet cannot imitate the justice of the divine examination, into which disturbance does not fall.

*Wherefore casting away,* etc. He has admonished them to seek out doctrine, for the receiving of which, and that they may be able to advance in it, he now exhorts to cleanness of body and of soul. For he who declines not from evil cannot do good. *The engrafted word.* That which by preaching we lay upon your hearts, or the word which was engrafted and sown in the day of redemption, when God begot you; now receive it more perfectly, and fulfil in works what you hold in mystery.

*To him that considereth the countenance.* He who purposes in his mind to consider in the Scriptures, as in a glass, the countenance of his nativity, how man is born, how frail, or what he shall be, of how brief an age, set in how many miseries, has contracted great compunction and a will of repenting; but straightway, seduced by some temptation, he forgets his compunction, and returns to sins. To this inconstancy he compares him who gladly hears the word and neglects to fulfil it. And there is a likeness between him who of his own accord, without a teacher, has applied himself to the Scriptures, and him who from another hears the Scriptures, since neither has fulfilled them.

When a boy is born he wails, whereby is signified the grief of the soul, and that it enters into life unto the miseries of the flesh, which grief the soul afterwards forgets, being accustomed to the enticements of the flesh.

*Not bridling his tongue,* etc. ((AUG., Serm. 3 ad fratres in eremo.)) What else is wordiness? etc., *as far as* and do thou diligently attend: *He that bridleth not his tongue, his religion is vain,* etc.

*And to keep himself unspotted from this world.* By *saeculum* he understands the world, or all the things which are in the world, as are the concupiscence of the flesh, and of the eyes, and the pride of life.

notes.text: Coming from Jerusalem — Probably on purpose to find occasion against him. Matt. xv, 1.
Washing of cups and pots and brazen vessels and couches — The Greek word (baptisms) means indifferently either washing or sprinkling. The cups, pots, and vessels were washed; the couches sprinkled.
The tradition of the elders — The rule delivered down from your forefathers.
Isaiah xxix, 13.

glossa.text: *And they come together. ((ID.))* It is plain how true is that confession of the Lord to the Father in which it is said: *Because thou hast hidden these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them to little ones ((Matth. XI))*. The unlearned come, they bring the sick, that they may touch even his hem, and therefore, having desired health, they suffer. But the Pharisees and the Scribes, who ought to have been the teachers of the people, run together not to hear the word, not as to a physician, but to the battles of questionings.

*With common hands. ((HIERON.))* By unclean, or common, hands he signifies the communion of the Gentiles. The cleanness of the Pharisees is barren; the communion of the apostles does not wholly stretch out its branches as far as the sea. *Not washed.* They find fault over the unwashed hands of the body, though in their works nothing of uncleanness is found. They themselves, washed outwardly with water, are inwardly polluted with the rancour of conscience.

*The Pharisees. ((BEDA.))* The superstitious tradition of men, to wash the oftener, for the sake of eating and the like. But the necessary teaching of truth bids those who desire to eat the bread of life which came down from heaven to cleanse their works by the frequent lament of alms and of the other fruits of justice.

*Washings.* In vain do they keep the washings of vessels, who neglect the filth of their own hearts and bodies. For this was not said of material hands, but for the cleansing of minds, and the chastisement of works, and the holiness and salvation of souls.

*Why do thy disciples,* etc. Wondrous folly! They accuse the Son of God because he does not keep the precepts of men. But the hands, that is, the works not of the body but of the soul, are to be washed, that the Word of God may be wrought in them.

*Well did he prophesy. ((HIERON.))* The fork of reason represses the barking of the Pharisees, that is, by the rebuke of Moses and of Isaias, that we too may be able to overcome heretics by the words of Scripture.

notes.text: The statutes — The laws which concern the worship and service of God. The judgments - The laws concerning your duties to men. So these two comprehend both tables, and the whole law of God.

glossa.text: *And now, O Israel, hear the precepts and the judgments. You shall not add.* He teaches the rule of equity, and strikes at every heresy. For he forbids to add anything of depraved intent to right doctrine, or to take away anything of the truth: for we must go by the royal way, not to the right hand or to the left; whence: *For the ways of the Lord are right, and the just shall walk in them ((Ose. XIV))*. In like manner John says: *If any man shall add to these things, God shall add unto him the plagues written in this book; if any man shall take away, God shall take away his part out of the book of life ((Apoc. XXII))*.

notes.text: Who — Who shall so dwell in thy church here, as to dwell with thee forever in heaven?

Uprightly — Loving, and serving God, and loving his neighbour not in word only, but in truth; and this constantly. Worketh - Makes it his business to do justly, to give to every one his due, first to God, and then to men. Speaketh - His words and professions to God and men, agree with the thoughts and purposes of his heart.

He — He that doth not speak evil of his neighbour. neighbour - That is, any man. Nor taketh - Into his mouth, doth not raise it, neither spread or propagate it; or believe it without sufficient reason.

Vile — An ungodly man. honoureth - He highly esteems and loves them, though they be mean as to their worldly condition, and though they may differ from him in some opinions or practices of lesser moment. Sweareth - A promissory oath. Hurt - To his own damage. As if a man solemnly swear, that he will sell him such an estate at a price below the full worth; or that, he will give a poor man such a sum of money, which afterwards he finds inconvenient to him. Changeth not - His purpose, but continues firm and resolved to perform his promise.

To usury — In such a manner as is contrary to God's law: of which see otherwise, Exod. xxii, 25 Levit xxv, 36, 37, &c. Reward - Or, a bribe for him who hath a bad cause. Moved - He shall abide with God here, and when he dies be forever with the Lord. David professes his trust in God, his adherence to him and love of his people, ver. 1-3. His satisfaction in God, ver. 4-7. He speaks in the person of Christ, of Gods presence with him, of his resurrection and the glory that should follow, ver. 8-11. Michtam of David. Title of the psalm. Michtam - This seems to be a title belonging to the musick or the song, which, with the rest, is now lost and unknown. As David was both a member, and an eminent type, of Christ, he speaks of himself sometimes in the one and sometimes in the other capacity: and therefore having spoken of himself as a member of Christ, in the former part of the psalm, he proceeds to consider himself as a type of Christ, and being inspired by the holy Ghost: towards the close he speaks such things, as though they might be accommodated to himself in a very imperfect sense, yet could not properly, belong to any but to Christ, to whom therefore they are justly appropriated in the New Testament.

glossa.text: *He that. ((Ibid.))* The answer of the Lord, etc. *as far as* as Christ the lamb, without breaking of members, who properly entered the temple, not that he might be expiated like the rest, but without stain. *He worketh justice.* As when he cast out of the temple those that sold and bought.

*He that speaketh.* Here he follows it out more fully. Truth is when the thing is so as it is said: this Christ did properly. *In his heart,* who at times kept silence toward the unworthy who questioned him fraudulently. *He hath not wrought deceit.* Deceit is in the tongue, when one thing is said and another is in the breast. Or, *he hath not wrought deceit,* because all that he heard from the Father, without any addition or suppression, he made known to his neighbours, that is, to the disciples; to the Jews, his neighbours according to the flesh. *Nor hath he done evil to his neighbour.* But he prayed for them; he did not take up reproach against his neighbours, as is plain from this, that he did not tear Judas with a biting rebuke.

*To nothing,* etc. ((AUG.)) This is perfection, that the malignant one avail nothing in a man, and that this be in his sight, that is, that he know for certain that no one is malignant save he who turns from the Creator to created things. *The malignant one,* that is, the devil, is despised; as when he said: *Go back, Satan,* etc. On the contrary, *he glorifieth them that fear the Lord.* He swore, when he promised the apostles with most certain truth: *Now I will not call you servants, but friends.*

*He that sweareth to his neighbour,* etc. ((Ibid.)) These three things are not great, etc., *as far as* since in the conclusion above he set down a past tense, *he is brought to nothing.*

*Money.* Either it is earthly, which is utterly forbidden to be given out at usury, and which the Lord handed over to Judas to be paid out to the poor, not for usury. Or it is spiritual, which is commanded to be given out at usury, that is, preaching for the instructing of men. *And gifts against the innocent.* Christ does indeed receive gifts, as from the Magi, and daily devout offerings; but not against the innocent; rather he gave his soul for them. *He that doeth these things shall not be moved.* Behold the complete answer to the questioner: he does them (he says), that he may invite us to the act, not only to the singing of them. *He that doeth these things shall not be moved.* ((CASS.)) The conclusion. In like manner he that doeth these things shall rest on the mountain.

This man - There is a peculiar force in the repetition of the word. Shall be happy - Not barely in hearing, but doing the will of God.

If any one be ever so religious — Exact in the outward offices of religion. And bridleth not his tongue - From backbiting, talebearing, evilspeaking, he only deceiveth his own heart, if he fancies he has any true religion at all.

The only true religion in the sight of God, is this, to visit — With counsel, comfort, and relief. The fatherless and widows - Those who need it most. In their affliction - In their most helpless and hopeless state. And to keep himself unspotted from the world - From the maxims, tempers, and customs of it. But this cannot be done, till we have given our hearts to God, and love our neighbour as ourselves.

glossa.text:
*Every gift,* etc. ((BED.)) After he had taught that vices are not to us from God, but from ourselves, etc., *as far as* the perfect gift can be understood.

*Nor of alteration.* No shadow shuts off his light, so as to send in any evils. Always the goods of light are in God, but his gifts in us are sometimes such as supervening sins overshadow.

*Of his own will.* Every good is from God, and you have not come to this by your own merits, but by the sole grace of the divine will. *That we might be some beginning,* etc. By this begetting let us not think that we are that which he himself is, but a certain primacy among creatures he granted to us by adoption. Whence another translator: *That we might be the firstfruits of his creatures.*

*Slow to anger.* Let no one be angry rashly and without cause, whether against sinning subjects, or against any brethren whatsoever, or against the prosperity of the wicked, because the ripeness of wisdom is not perceived save with a tranquil mind. And he who judges in anger, even if he judges justice, yet cannot imitate the justice of the divine examination, into which disturbance does not fall.

*Wherefore casting away,* etc. He has admonished them to seek out doctrine, for the receiving of which, and that they may be able to advance in it, he now exhorts to cleanness of body and of soul. For he who declines not from evil cannot do good. *The engrafted word.* That which by preaching we lay upon your hearts, or the word which was engrafted and sown in the day of redemption, when God begot you; now receive it more perfectly, and fulfil in works what you hold in mystery.

*To him that considereth the countenance.* He who purposes in his mind to consider in the Scriptures, as in a glass, the countenance of his nativity, how man is born, how frail, or what he shall be, of how brief an age, set in how many miseries, has contracted great compunction and a will of repenting; but straightway, seduced by some temptation, he forgets his compunction, and returns to sins. To this inconstancy he compares him who gladly hears the word and neglects to fulfil it. And there is a likeness between him who of his own accord, without a teacher, has applied himself to the Scriptures, and him who from another hears the Scriptures, since neither has fulfilled them.

When a boy is born he wails, whereby is signified the grief of the soul, and that it enters into life unto the miseries of the flesh, which grief the soul afterwards forgets, being accustomed to the enticements of the flesh.

*Not bridling his tongue,* etc. ((AUG., Serm. 3 ad fratres in eremo.)) What else is wordiness? etc., *as far as* and do thou diligently attend: *He that bridleth not his tongue, his religion is vain,* etc.

*And to keep himself unspotted from this world.* By *saeculum* he understands the world, or all the things which are in the world, as are the concupiscence of the flesh, and of the eyes, and the pride of life.

notes.text: Coming from Jerusalem — Probably on purpose to find occasion against him. Matt. xv, 1.
Washing of cups and pots and brazen vessels and couches — The Greek word (baptisms) means indifferently either washing or sprinkling. The cups, pots, and vessels were washed; the couches sprinkled.
The tradition of the elders — The rule delivered down from your forefathers.
Isaiah xxix, 13.

glossa.text: *And they come together. ((ID.))* It is plain how true is that confession of the Lord to the Father in which it is said: *Because thou hast hidden these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them to little ones ((Matth. XI))*. The unlearned come, they bring the sick, that they may touch even his hem, and therefore, having desired health, they suffer. But the Pharisees and the Scribes, who ought to have been the teachers of the people, run together not to hear the word, not as to a physician, but to the battles of questionings.

*With common hands. ((HIERON.))* By unclean, or common, hands he signifies the communion of the Gentiles. The cleanness of the Pharisees is barren; the communion of the apostles does not wholly stretch out its branches as far as the sea. *Not washed.* They find fault over the unwashed hands of the body, though in their works nothing of uncleanness is found. They themselves, washed outwardly with water, are inwardly polluted with the rancour of conscience.

*The Pharisees. ((BEDA.))* The superstitious tradition of men, to wash the oftener, for the sake of eating and the like. But the necessary teaching of truth bids those who desire to eat the bread of life which came down from heaven to cleanse their works by the frequent lament of alms and of the other fruits of justice.

*Washings.* In vain do they keep the washings of vessels, who neglect the filth of their own hearts and bodies. For this was not said of material hands, but for the cleansing of minds, and the chastisement of works, and the holiness and salvation of souls.

*Why do thy disciples,* etc. Wondrous folly! They accuse the Son of God because he does not keep the precepts of men. But the hands, that is, the works not of the body but of the soul, are to be washed, that the Word of God may be wrought in them.

*Well did he prophesy. ((HIERON.))* The fork of reason represses the barking of the Pharisees, that is, by the rebuke of Moses and of Isaias, that we too may be able to overcome heretics by the words of Scripture.

registers.label: Spare
lines: The voice of my beloved! Look, he comes leaping over the hills.
Arise, my love, and come away.
The winter is past, the rains are over and gone.
The flowers appear; the time of singing has come.
Every good and perfect gift is from above.
We come to receive, and to be doers of the word.
Come away from your locked rooms; come, let us worship.
The time of singing has come. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: Listen, the voice of your beloved, bounding over the mountains, calling through the lattice: rise up and come away with me.
The winter is past; the time of singing has come.
The cold gray season is over, the rain has stopped, the ground is thick with flowers, and the voice of the turtledove is back in the land.
The winter is past; the time of singing has come.
Every good and perfect gift comes down from the Father of lights, in whom there is no shifting shadow, only steady morning.
The winter is past; the time of singing has come.
So come out of whatever wintered you; be quick to listen, slow to anger, doers of the word, and sing.
The winter is past; the time of singing has come, and we have come to sing.

registers.label: Hybrid
lines: The voice of the beloved: arise and come away.
The time of singing has come.
Winter is over; the flowers are on the earth.
The time of singing has come.
Every good gift comes down from the Father of lights.
The time of singing has come.
